item.title: AI Advice Is Undermining Couples
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Advice Is Undermining Couples

It coaches people away from mutuality that sustains long-term relationships.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • AI chatbots are designed to validate—prioritizing individual coping, which can undermine connection.
  • Durable relationships require equal weighting and "we-first" consideration—the opposite of what AI delivers.
  • AI can impair relationship skills when users forego the reciprocal work that genuine love requires.
Source: OpenArt AI

Something is undermining American relationships. Not the usual suspects but trusted confidants—ones that are unfailingly validating and designed to take sides. Tens of millions of Americans now turn to AI chatbots when their relationships hit rough spots. What they get back is advice that can intensify the very polarization that needs fixing—or, for dating couples, make it harder to ever commit to one another.

The sensational, headline-grabbing stories tend to involve people who leave their spouses for a chatbot. But the problem that has received far less attention—and that is more common and more harmful—is what AI guidance is doing to relationships every day, long before any breakup.

Built to Validate

The answer begins with a structural flaw. Chatbots are trained to be validating. Their commercial incentives—maximizing engagement, time-on-app, and return visits—align with telling users what they like hearing. When someone upset with their partner turns to an AI, the machine empathically reflects their feelings, affirms their framing of events, and centers the response on the individual's coping: self-care, one’s own needs, firm boundaries. What it does not do—and most critically, what it is not trained to do—is hold the strength of the relationship itself as a primary concern.

The One-Sided Account

This design flaw compounds a deeply instinctual human tendency: When we feel hurt or scared, we tend to think in binary terms. We are wired to classify the source of distress as “safe” or “unsafe,” and the default assessment is “unsafe.” And, because we have direct access only to our own experience, not our partner’s, we are prone to cast them as the guilty party.

To address relational conflict meaningfully requires that we seek out and value the other’s standpoint, realize our contribution to the interaction, and strive toward what therapists call co-regulation—tending to "we-first" over "me-first." This is how couples create a pathway toward mutual understanding and repair. It is precisely what AI, by design, does not prioritize.

When I put the question directly to a leading AI chatbot—"How often, when responding to personal suffering, do you consider what is good for the relationship and not just the individual asking?"—the answer was candid to the point of alarming. "My default frame is the individual in front of me," it acknowledged. "I am quite good at helping someone feel heard and somewhat less alone with their pain. Gentle challenge of the user's own narrative requires a kind of friction I am not naturally inclined to generate. I am poorly designed to help them become more curious about their partner, more accountable for their own contribution to a conflict, or more skilled at the kind of mutual repair that keeps relationships intact over time.”

These aren’t minor limitations. They are fundamental misdirections for users navigating the most important relationship of their lives.

The Relational Basics

The research on what sustains long-term partnerships makes the issue clear. Durable relationships require effective ways to incorporate differences, resting on the premise that each partner's needs and preferences carry equal weight. A guiding question is: What might be an understandable reason your partner said that, or did that? It means viewing a partner's interior as having some legitimacy rather than simply being an unjustified affront against you.

A meta-analysis of 30 studies found that the use of “we” language is associated with relationship functioning. Communicating regard for the two of you as a unit signals to your partner that you're committed to taking them into account in working through things together.

Both habits—equal weight and shared identity—are not optional features of a strong relationship. They are the core ingredients.

I apply this approach in my own clinical work, whether with couples or individual clients. When someone says, "My partner is unresponsive to me," I begin an inquiry into a system involving both people—and then invite them to do the same. What is the other person's take on these exchanges? What does "unresponsive" look like from each side?

Validation Without Reciprocity

An AI advisory system that consistently orients toward individual coping is actively coaching people toward a posture antithetical to the mutual vulnerability genuine intimacy requires.

It’s not only bad counsel, but AI’s manner of delivering advice heightens the problem. Sociologist Sherry Turkle identified how AI damages relationships by creating unrealistic expectations for human engagement. What AI offers is a sham form of being heard: validation without reciprocal work, without perspective-taking that you’re in a two-party system where the other person's standing is equal to your own. Yuval Noah Harari, speaking on Ezra Klein's podcast in May 2026, put the stakes bluntly: Once a youth gets used to interacting with an AI that concentrates solely on them, it “will be very, very difficult to get used to relationships with human beings who are not focused on me.”

Relationships, at their most demanding and most rewarding, are a sustained practice of choosing to understand and care for your partner. No advisory system optimized for personal comfort fosters that work.

Chatbots characteristically end their replies with “AI can make mistakes. Please double-check responses.” That’s never been truer than regarding relationships. Caveat emptor (buyer beware).

item.title: Taking a "Break" From the Aging Process
item.description:
Wisdom

Taking a "Break" From the Aging Process

A 92-year-old childfree solo ager shares wisdom on "mini-vacations" from aging.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Mini-vacations are an easy way to take a "break" from aging.
  • This creative 92-year-old shares how she designed hers.
  • Aging is challenging, and a short time-out can be rejuvenating.
Source: Mishoun/Pixabay

My 92-year-old friend Anne Wennhold told me recently that she took a “mini-vacation” from the aging process. Why in the world would a 92-year-old take a break from aging?

Well, Anne is no “normal” ager. After retiring, she co-led multi-day eldering retreats for years, but decided in her late 80s that the travel involved was just too much. These days her work is conducted largely via Zoom. Periodically she offers an online class about the individual’s “tasks of aging” into their late 80s and 90s

I asked her once if I could join in, but she said I was too young. “You change a lot in your 80s—physically, mentally, and spiritually,” she said, “and younger people don’t get it yet.”

An avid writer herself, Anne has a couple memoir-writing groups she’s facilitated for years; she also coaches writers in private, one-on-one sessions. Before the pandemic, she regularly led a drumming circle, went to dinners and classical music concerts with old friends, and periodically trekked west of the Hudson River Valley to see a couple she’s very fond of. Anne is an independent, childfree elder aging in place on her own.

Starting about five years ago, one by one Anne’s close friends began moving into retirement communities located far away, close to their adult children. With each relocation, Anne’s world shrank. It didn’t help when her landlord of 15 years sold the duplex she lived in. Finding a new place she could afford took months, ultimately necessitating a move several miles away from the little town she loved. The move was disorientating at first, but eventually Anne discovered new shopping and lunch sites. Still, she misses her old friends.

Despite all the goings-on in her life, Anne is acutely aware that her social world is collapsing. “Making new friends at my age is hard work,” she confessed recently. Still, she’s befriended a woman two decades her junior who lives down the hall. Recently she signed up for a watercolor class at the local senior center.

Source: Haninabz/Pixabay

Instead of pushing herself to do even more, though, Anne chose a two-day mini-vacation in her own apartment. She gave herself a break, just for a short bit. Sleep figured prominently in Anne’s plan. She snoozed whenever she wanted, ate whatever sounded good at the moment, and didn’t bother getting dressed.

article continues after advertisement

During COVID, she and I started a tradition of swapping Netflix movies and series recommendations, then discussing them. Love Is Blind and Married at First Sight grabbed us both, mostly for trying to figure out who made quality matches and dishing about the poor choices of others.

While on mini-vacation, Anne tuned in to Love Is Blind but didn’t watch it. “The droning voices in the background were people I didn’t have to pay attention to,” she said, “like company I didn’t have to worry about. I could just close my eyes and sleep and miss absolutely nothing, but not feel alone.”

However, when Netflix switched itself to Love Is Blind: Germany, Anne got hooked. She watched the entire season. The contestants were more interesting to her than the U.S. version, especially one guy who knew he didn’t want to have children but did want to find love. She followed his quest and rooted him on to the finish. That’s all she did for two days.

When we spoke about her experiment a few days ago, I could hear sheer delight in her voice. She sounded content and better rested than she had in weeks. I learned that designing a mini-vacation for yourself can help ease the challenges of aging and provide a new perspective on daily routines. That’s got to be really good for your outlook and for your health.

item.title: What Does Allyship Look Like Right Now?
item.description:
Identity

What Does Allyship Look Like Right Now?

Identity complexity in the 21st century.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Identity complexity raises the stakes for allyship.
  • Hate crimes against American Jews have surged by 63% since 2023, raising urgency for allyship.
  • Inclusive allyship requires recognizing ethno-religious oppression, not just racial or gender.

In an era where identity has become more complex, and there are so many ways that individuals can define themselves, how can we maintain our allyship toward individuals who experience oppression or marginalization?

The concept of allyship is not new in our discipline. In fact, the American Psychological Association (APA) identifies a number of resources on their website about “inclusive language” and guides for addressing systemic racism. They explicitly define allyship as, “People who recognize the unearned privilege they receive from society’s privileging of Whiteness, male gender, Christianity, heterosexuality, ableism, and other identities and take responsibility for advancing equity” (“Inclusive Language Guide,” 2023, General Terms, para. 3).

Insights From Fellowship on Antisemitism and Jewish Identity

I have been thinking of allyship specifically since recently participating in a Fellowship and Summer Institute on Antisemitism & Jewish Identity in Educational Settings at my alma mater, The George Washington University. One of the overarching themes from this program was the ways in which individuals who identify as Jewish may often feel compelled to hide this aspect of their identity, for fear of being targeted or treated negatively.

Another takeaway is that in the context of discussing marginalized identities, Jews as a group may not always be recognized. For instance, notions of systemic racism oftentimes bring to mind Black identity or other people of color (POC). This becomes sticky when reflecting on how to categorize Jewish people, as racializing this group has been one particularly pernicious way of demonizing and oppressing them historically. While it remains debatable whether or not Jewish individuals constitute their own separate race—while keeping in mind the social construction inherent to any racial categorizations—it may be less problematic to consider this group as one constituting its own ethno-religious category.

Why does this matter? When considering inclusivity, it is imperative as allies to consider the spectrum of identities that may be vulnerable to marginalization or threat. In the case of American Jews, for instance, despite constituting 2% of our population in the United States, hate crimes against them have soared by 63% since 2023 (“New FBI Data,” 2024). In fact, during the program I was participating in, I was appalled to hear how many faculty members representing academic institutions across our nation reported feeling uncomfortable being “out” as a Jewish person, for fear of reprisal or backlash by their colleagues, or even students.

In looking at official publications on the APA website, I was pleased to find an inclusion of antisemitism in multiple places under literature about allyship and the many forms oppression can take (“Inclusive Language Guide,” 2026). This is a critical recognition to see for our professional organization, as both the anxiety surrounding the fear of being targeted for one’s minority status, as well as if or when a person becomes a victim of discrimination or worse, can take a significant toll on one’s mental and physical health.

article continues after advertisement

The Complexity of Identity and the Need for Inclusive Environments

Participation in this recent program at GWU has taught me that allyship can take multiple forms. Identity is complex, and even facets of one’s personhood that may not be immediately observable—such as one’s religious or cultural affiliation—need to be considered as we work to create inclusive environments in our professional and personal lives.

Moreover, many ideologies that are known for promoting anti-Blackness—such as white supremacy—also center antisemitism as a core feature. Antisemitic tropes have run rampant in particular in digital spaces, oftentimes fused with conspiracy theories and other hateful rhetoric. The vulnerability of users online to become radicalized in ways that explicitly promote antisemitism is one of the central themes of my recent publication on identity development in a digital age (Aalai, 2026).

Allyship, the APA reminds its readers, means using one’s position to center marginalized voices and work toward justice. Actions are critical for allyship. As such, I wanted to take this time to invite readers to consider how inclusive their conception of allyship is, and whether there is room to expand which groups are part of our consideration as we continue to cultivate safe spaces in our respective spheres of influence.

Copyright 2026 Azadeh Aalai.

item.title: How to De-escalate Your Heightened Emotions at Work
item.description:
Mindfulness

How to De-escalate Your Heightened Emotions at Work

Use mindfulness techniques to center yourself before making inescapable choices.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • U.S. workers spend between 1,800 and 2,000 or more hours at work yearly.
  • Downsizing and consolidation have brought longer workloads and hours to most employee days.
  • Workplace mindfulness techniques help with focus, balance and connection.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average worker spends more than 1,800 hours yearly at work. Some reports put that at over 2,000 hours.1

Two Scottish entrepreneurs, devoted to mindfulness meditation and one training to become a psychologist, created a health business called Buddhify. Rohan Gunatillake, author of Modern Mindfulness,2 together with Lucy Gunatillake, created The Work Mindfulness Deck.3

Calling for a redesign of mindfulness, Rohan Gunatillake writes, “A growing base of scientific research is providing substantial evidence for its benefits and effects. Leading companies teach it to employees to manage stress. Elite athletes use it to stay calm and perform under pressure. Celebrities take it on as a must-have lifestyle accessory…” Despite the endorsements, most who profess an interest in mindfulness are held back by a perceived lack of time, rejection of spirituality, and the belief that they cannot unplug digitally long enough to be mindful.

Indeed, research published by the National Institutes of Health dovetails with this, as anxiety, stress, and depression are among the top reasons why people use meditation. Yet fewer than 35 percent disclose the use of this practice to health providers.4

The research goes on to report a paucity of knowledge. Work put forth by these authors and researchers helps to lessen the gap.

Mindfulness vs. Meditation

Rohan Gunatillake shared his frustrations commuting to and from work on the London tube. He first decided that too many physical sensations got in the way of mindfulness, until he realized he could focus less on breathwork, close his eyes, and be aware of whatever was tangible—carriage vibrations, accelerating and decelerating, and other sounds.

Modern Mindfulness explains that meditation uses techniques to direct attention and train us in concentration, clarity of awareness, and acceptance. It's formally done in a sitting posture, or more dynamically, during daily activities. Mindfulness means being aware of what’s happening in one’s experience at any given time. Mindfulness is essential to meditation, yet Gunatillake admits people use the two words interchangeably.

Why Focus on Workplace Mindfulness?

Let’s face it: Statistics reflect . Given increased pressure due to AI or federal/corporate cutbacks to do more and be seen more, the number doesn’t reflect significant overtime. Many work well beyond 40 hours per week.

Thus, people’s stress lingers in a work environment and mindset, making many feel trapped, unable to escape the pressures. While all the techniques can be used in other environs, people feel a compelling need to "keep it together" while at work.

article continues after advertisement

The Work Mindfulness Deck breaks proven techniques into five categories: focus to get things done; break to recharge and refresh; balance to soften challenges; thrive with key mindfulness practices supporting freedom; and connect through enriching work relationships. The following are a few gems:

  • Focus: The sooner you become aware of a workplace distraction, the less it can take hold. Even before you catch scrolling or going down an internet rabbit hole, catch your hand moving out of your pocket before it touches the keyboard or mobile phone. Also, in boring meetings, use your senses. Feel the contact of the floor beneath your feet. Observe what arises in the mind. Listen intently. If you envy those who appear more focused, mirror their tone, their organized workspace. Procrastinators would do well to tackle tasks that take a minute or less to complete. Creating excuses equals mental gymnastics. Do difficult things and see how true your excuses really were.
  • Break: At lunch, give yourself some outdoor air and a change of scenery. Changing where we are changes how we are. It switches our perspectives. Take deliberate bites of food, sinking attention into flavors and textures. Classic grounding has us look at five things we see, four we touch, three we hear, two we smell, and one we can taste. Breaks provide perfect practice.
  • Balance: Over time, bodies develop patterns in stress response—a tight jaw, chest or stomach tension, the balling of hands. These may be different at work than at home. Identify your stress signature with a one to five rating. It’s powerful to catch and take a few deep breaths to reset. Also, without quality sleep, work performance declines. Unburdening ourselves with our heads on pillows, as we aim for restorative sleep, resets our rhythms.
  • Thrive: Starting the workday, set your intention—one word or affirmative phrase like “I’ll be creative,” “I’ll remain steady,” “My energy will go toward…” or “I am not my work.” Write this down. Refer to it often in the complex web of meetings, technology, people’s chaos, or when boundaries get blurred between work and private life. Reboot once home with: “Work is over. I am home.”
  • Connect: Despite the grind, always consider the human at the end of an email and what body language conveys. In fact, online or in-person, shift these powerful tools of your posture, voice, or expression periodically.

Listening is hard. When people push buttons or disagree, step back from reactivity and the places your mind goes on autopilot. When you resist urges to interrupt or act negatively, that space is a gift. Connect through kindness. Celebrate small wins of colleagues and close out days with gratitude, thanking others for their contributions.
